headline: Mayor approved accepting approximately $330,000 annually for five years from the Go North Initiative.
summary: Staff reported that measles cases are rising nationally and that Nashua wastewater levels are elevated, while flu and respiratory illness remain low in New Hampshire. A $10,000 grant from NHCF will help people who do not qualify for Welfare, and the Welfare Department reported rising rental costs and individuals discharged into homelessness. The October 2026 minutes were also approved.

plain_text:
Page 1 of 4 
 
 
 
Board of Health 
November 18, 2026 
18 Mulberry Street 
Nashua, NH 03060 
12:30 PM 
Our mission is to promote, protect, and preserve the health and well-being of the Greater Nashua Region 
through leadership and community collaboration. Our vision is to have an informed, safe, healthy, and 
resilient community where all people can thrive and prosper. We subscribe to the following values: integrity, 
leadership, adaptability, and respect. 
Facilitator: Board Chair, Dr Charles 
Cappetta   
Minutes 
Attendees 
Board of Health (BOH):  Dr. Charles Cappetta, Stephanie Ballentine, Christian Jimenez; 
Henry Och 
Board of Alderman:  
City Employees: Bobbie D Bagley, Director DPHCS; Heidi Peek-Kukulka, Health Officer; 
Mike McGuiness, Deputy Health Officer; Kim Bernard, Chief Public Health Nurse, Bob 
Mack, Welfare Officer; Foqia Ijaz, CS Administrative Assistant; Sakshi Gurung, 
Epidemiologist  
Updates and Announcements 
Meeting Called 
to Order 
 
Board Chair, Dr. Cappetta called the meeting to order at 12: 30 P.M referencing NH RSA 
91-A:2, II.  
Approval of 
Minutes 
October, 2026 
• Approved   
Director’s Report  
Presented by 
Bobbie Bagley, 
Director DPHCS 
 
• DPHCS vision and mission were read.  
• NHCF reached out regarding a $10,000 funding to assist individuals in the 
community who face barriers to accessing financial assistance. The funding will 
help individuals who do not qualify for Welfare or other assistance programs, 
particularly with housing-related expenses and gaps in payments. We have 
approximately six months to spend the funds. The $10,000 grant will be
Page 2 of 4 
 
coordinated with Welfare and other community agencies. The funds must be spent 
by December 31. 
• Go North Initiative: Public Health was previously not eligible to apply but is now 
able to participate through PHN. The initiative provides approximately $330,000 
annually. Mayor has approved to accept the funding. We will contract with 
Endowment for Health to be the fiscal agent for that funding. The funding is for 
five years and will require a contract. The goal is to develop additional regional 
support and strengthen community engagement. 
• National Association of Local Boards of Health Conference: The conference was 
insightful and focused on advocacy and support for local Boards of Health. The CDC 
Surgeon General spoke about concerns regarding funding cuts, particularly around 
the election period, and how local public health departments can be supported. 
The importance of effectively presenting data was emphasized. Economic and 
geographic burdens should be highlighted when discussing public health issues. 
GLP-1 medication costs were discussed, particularly the financial barriers for 
individuals who cannot afford them. The group discussed leveraging trusted 
community members, hospitals, and other community agencies to strengthen 
public health efforts. Data collection was also highlighted as an important priority. 
• CS Departmental Reports: Community Health Workers data includes client 
interactions, referrals, and other services provided to support individuals 
experiencing homelessness. 
• Housing Services officer is working on onboarding, Resource Center activities, and 
the Homeless Services Gap Analysis. 
• The Warming Station opened on November 16 and is operating well, with new 
individuals accessing services and staff collecting data on substance use and 
housing needs. Resource Center visits are slowly increasing, with the most 
requested services being housing, employment, transportation, and general 
assistance, and fentanyl remains the most commonly reported substance. 
 
Epidemiologist 
Report Presented 
by Sakshi Gurung 
Measles Report:  
• The United States is experiencing an increase in measles cases, with approximately 
5412 confirmed and suspected cases reported across 47 states as of November 11, 
2026, the highest total in 35 years. The increase is attributed to both interstate and 
local transmission, declining MMR vaccination rates, and an increase in travel-
related cases. Vermont department of health issued a HAN and also reported small 
number of cases.  
• Updates on measles cases in Mexico and Canada were also given. 
Respiratory Illness and Flu Update in New Hampshire: 
• Week 43, weekly seasonal respiratory virus report – 1.9% patient visit for Influenza 
like illness, 4.9% of Visits for Acute respiratory Illness, Pneumonia and influenza 
related death 2.7%.  
• CDC data showed low levels of respiratory illness in New Hampshire. COVID-19 
activity was also low. 
• Wastewater Surveillance: Nashua showed elevated and increasing levels, while 
Merrimack remained low and stable.
Page 3 of 4 
 
• Updates were provided on completed activities, meetings, and other epidemiology 
initiatives. 
CH Department 
Report provided 
by Chief PH Nurse 
Kim Bernard 
 
• Flu clinics have been very busy. 
• CH is partnering with other organizations to offer additional flu clinics. 
• The quarterly medical providers meeting included discussions about current 
healthcare issues, including injectable HIV PrEP. The department plans to roll 
out this service soon. 
• Hepatitis C Program: 
o The first Hepatitis C client returned an undetected result. 
o The program is receiving numerous referrals and is looking to expand 
services and increase referrals from community partners. 
o The program focuses on individuals who may otherwise fall through the 
cracks and have difficulty accessing services. 
o Dr. Cappetta expressed interest in attending the medical providers 
meeting. Kim will invite Dr. Cappetta. 
•  Continue to support nursing student for public health experiences as part of 
workforce development.  
Environmental 
Health (EH) 
Department 
report provided 
by Health Officer 
–Heidi Peek-
Kukulka 
• Seven reinspection’s were conducted. 
• Rodent issues continue to be a concern. EH is working to educate property owners 
and identify appropriate cleaning methods to prevent recurring problems. 
• If facilities do not comply with requirements, the conditions may become a public 
health hazard, and the department may need to consider enforcement through 
local ordinances.  
• The department's software was down for a period of time and has since been 
updated to a newer version. However, the new system requires more manual 
work, so the department is exploring other affordable software options. The 
department plans purchase new software for the next fiscal year. Staff are also 
working to become familiar with the updated system. 
• The Holiday Stroll is the biggest event of the year for Environmental Health. A large 
number of vendors are expected, and two staff members will work extended hours 
to support the event. 
• The department is reviewing its budget and looking for ways to reduce expenses. 
Pool testing kits are very expensive, so EH is evaluating whether certain tests can 
be eliminated. The department plans to conduct some of the more expensive state 
testing on an as-needed basis, particularly when an illness or other concern is 
reported. 
• Environmental Health is monitoring several LSR’s listed on the NH General Court 
website, including proposed legislation related to occasional food service 
establishments, xylazine classification, and kratom classification. 
Welfare 
Department 
report provided 
• General Assistance requests continue to be driven primarily by rental and shelter 
needs. Although one additional voucher was issued compared to last year, costs 
increased by approximately $13,000 due to rising rental prices. A slight decrease in
Page 4 of 4 
 
by Bob Mack, 
Welfare Officer  
requests is expected during the winter months, and the utility disconnection 
moratorium will begin soon. Staff continue referring clients to other agencies for 
additional support and emergency assistance. Refer to the report for updated 
numbers. 
• The department continues to face challenges assisting individuals with complex 
medical conditions or mobility limitations, particularly when hospitals seek help 
with discharge planning. Some individuals are discharged into homelessness 
because shelters cannot accommodate their medical needs and hospitals are not 
responsible for long-term placement. Staff work with CHWs and other agencies to 
connect individuals with available services while continuing advocacy efforts for 
those who need a higher level of care. The group discussed the Homeless Services 
Gap Analysis, the availability of VNA services, unsafe discharges, and the need for 
stronger community support. The department plans to raise these concerns with 
the Commissioner and Hospital Association, and the Board of Health may also be 
asked to assist with advocacy. The Bureau of Adult Protective Services was also 
identified as a potential resource. 
Other Updates  • The Board chair wished a Happy Thanksgiving to those who celebrate.  
Public Comment • A Nashua Community College student thanked the department for its work and acknowledged the efforts being made to support the community. 
 
The meeting adjourned at 1:39 PM following a motion and vote. 
 
Please join us for our Next Meeting: 
November 18, 2026 at 12:30 PM
